subject: Distance analysis question on nested design.

messages.author: 9bbb4617ab77661e
messages.subject: Distance analysis question on nested design.
parts:
I have a rather complex distance analysis that I hope you can be of some
assistance in setting it up for analysis in program Distance. The project
is a multi species study estimating the density of arboreal rodent nest
structures. There are 5 species of arboreal rodents and the rarer species,
which are the most interesting to us, do not have sufficient detections to
model a detection function using just their detections. Therefore, I was
planning on using all the nests in a global model to estimate the detection
function and than post stratify by species. However our sampling design
also has three strata (conifer stand age\structure classes) in which we
randomly selected a number of conifer stands to sample in each strata. In
each stand we conducted line transect sampling where the lines were laid
out with a random start and within a stand each transect was divided into
2 =96 3 independent segments.

Given Program Distance=92s current limit on analysis of nested designs, I wa=
s
considering using the stand types (3 levels) as a factor covariate and
running an analysis. What I=92m not sure of is if this is the best approach=

and which options I need to use to obtain the correct standard error
estimates. I would like to have density estimates at both strata level
(each stand type) and at the individual stand level for each species.
Given that all the stands within a stratum were randomly selected from a
larger population of such stands in the study area and that there were
multiple independent transect segments in each stand sampled, I though that
this approach would be statistically valid. However, I=92m not sure how to
set it up. I also assume that program distance may not be able to
calculate all the estimates and that I may have to calculate part of them
outside the program. But I=92m not sure of the correct formula.

I would appreciate any advice that you can provide on this analysis.

--

messages.author: 4b4a7b00c1dd09c7
messages.subject: Re: Distance analysis question on nested design.
parts:
Hi Brian, list,

Let's start by ignoring species, and focus on the analysis for a single
species for which you have enough samples to fit a detection function. This
means using the data selection part of the data filter in Distance to get
only data for that species.

I'll also assume for now that either (a) within each stratum, all stands are
the same area, or (b) that you selected the random sample of stands within
each stratum with probability proportional to stand area and that within
each selected stand transect line length is proportional to stand area.
Either (a) or (b) mean that you have even coverage probability within
stratum (each point in a stratum has the same probability of being sampled).

For getting estimates of density and standard errors at the stratum level,
and estimates at the stand level, it seems to me you can pool your transects
(someone out there correct me if you disagree). In this view, the stand is
the random sample for estimating variance in encounter rate. You simply
pool observations across transects within stands, and make the stand the
"sample" layer in Distance. You then proceed as normal, fitting detection
functions etc, and estimating density at the stratum and sample (stand)
level. Note that to get abundance at the stand level, you'll need to
multiply the density estiamtes by the stand area as Distance will only give
you the abundance within the sampled strips at the sample level.

The only thing you can't get out of the above is estimates of the standard
error of density at the stand level, since you've pooled the transects
together. I might be wrong in reading what you wrote but it seemed to imply
that you only had 2-3 "independent segments" per stand -- in this case you
won't be able to estimate a valid SE at the stand level in any case.

If I'm wrong and you do have lots of independent transects at the stand
level, then you can still do it in Distance, one of two ways:
(1) If your detection function is global, or you've used stratum as a
covariate then you can still do it in Distance. Set up a new project in
which stand is the stratum layer, and your transects are at the sample
level. You'll need your old strata in there as a field if you want to use
them as a covariate. Then set up the same detection function as previously,
and get a density estimate by stratum layer (i.e., by stand). This should
be the same as the previous density estiamtes, but now you have a valid SE.
Note that the global density estimate in this case is garbage so ignore it.
(2) If your detection function for this species was by stratum, then you can
set up a similar project to (1), but set up 3 data filters, one for each
stratum (or you could have 3 distance projects). Then for each stratum, do
an analysis with a global detection function and the density estimate and SE
by "stratum" (i.e., by stand) are what you want.

Now, what about that species for which you had too few detections to model
separately? A few options here. The first is to treat the whole question
of whether to estimate a separate detection function for each species, to
use a factor covariate for each species or to pool some or all together just
like any other model selection problem (e.g., what to do about your strata),
and to try all the options and use AIC to guide you. This assumes you have
no problems in the data that mean that AIC is not reliable. The usual
bias/variance arguments apply -- although in this case it's most common that
there really are quite large differences in detection function between many
species so the bias can be quite large. Also, in your case you'll be
constrained in that some species (the rare one) cannot be treated
separately.

If you end up with species as a stratum in the detection function (except
the rare one), you're back with treating each species separately as above.
If species is a covariate, then estimating the appropriate SE for each
species isn't possible analytically using the output that Distance gives
you. Rather, you'd have to boostrap. In your example I expect you'd want
to bootstrap by stand and possibly also by transect within stand (assuming
you have enough transects within each stand to do this). You'd have to
program that bootstrap outside of Distance, calling the MCDS.exe analysis
engine to fit the detection functions -- I've posted on this previously.

So, on balance, you may want to stick to fitting each species separately
apart from the one where you don't have enough data. For this rare species,
you then need to get a detection function from somewhere -- probably by
bringing in data from a species (or more) that you judge to have similar
detectability. Note that this obviously means you have to interpret the
density estimates (and CIs) with a pinch of salt. You can fit the detection
function to the combined data, and then use multipliers to apply this
funciton to only the data from the rare species to get the appropriate
density and SE (see Multipliers in the Distance online manual for how to do
this). Will work fine for global and by stratum detection functions, but
not for species as a covariate.

OK, so what if you didn't sample in proportion to stand area, or put the
same number of transects in each stand regardless of it's area. Then you
have less sample coverage in larger stands, and the standard methods in
Distance for computing encounter rate and ER variance won't work. Also, you
don't have pooling robustness any more (although perheaps it's not that
likely that detection function varies in relation to stand area -- unless
there's a big edge effect). For calculating density (ie ignoring the
detection function part) there are two issues: one is selection of stands
and the other is coverage of transects within stands. If you simply took a
random sample of stands and they vary greatly in size and if you think that
density may vary by stand area (e.g., density lower in smaller stands due to
edge effects) you'd better take this into account at the analysis stage.
You can get stratum encounter rate as an weighted mean of the stand
encounter rates, where the weighting is by stand area. Variance in
encounter rate is then the variance of a weighted mean. Density can then be
calculated using the standard formulae (Distance book page 76). If you used
the same sample length in each stand then this is less of a big deal -- you
didn't allocate effort optimally (you usually want effort proportional to
abundance) so may get less efficiency, but the standard Distance analysis I
outlined in the 3rd paragraph, above, can cope with this (bit like visiting
some lines more than once - Distance book page 79).

Sorry for the long answer, but hope it helps,

- Len
